source_text: Quia maior et minor ad finitam speciem pertinet quantitatis? Sed quantitas non solum contrariorum capax non est, quod ei cum qualitate atque aliis praedicamentis; verum etiam nec contrarium habet, quod ei cum substantiae est definitione commune: bonum vero et malum contraria sunt
pass_a_gloss: Because greater and lesser to finitam speciem pertinet quantitatis? but quantitas not only contrariorum capable not is, that/which to-him when/with qualitate and aliis praedicamentis; true also nor contrarium has, that/which to-him when/with of-substance is definitione commune: good but and evil contrary are.

lemmas.lexica: LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: ‘Greater’ and ‘lesser’ belong to the defined category of quantity. But quantity is not only incapable of receiving contraries—which it has in common with quality and other categories—it also has no contrary, which it has in common with the definition of substance. Good and evil, however, are contraries.

choices.why: Keep Julian's good-of-nature vs good-of-will contrast; do not baptize as 'grace'.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
